title: Dual certificates and a scalar inner solver for the minimum compensation budget
scope: Convex dual characterization, constructive inner minimization and sensitivity of the source's training-and-transfer compensation model.
significance: Gives an exact dual frontier with shadow costs of each compensation floor and reduces every dual inner problem to one monotone scalar equation.
body:
# Dual certificates and a scalar inner solver for compensation

The manuscript's minimum-budget theorem is correct. Its subgradient multipliers also yield an exact dual representation and a practical reduction of the inner optimization to one scalar. This provides global budget certificates and interprets which workers' losses constrain the policy.

Retain all primitives in “Workers, training and fiscal costs.” For \(\lambda\in[0,1]^N\), put \(D_\lambda=\sum_i\lambda_id_i\), \(X=\sum_ix_i\), and
\[
L(x,\lambda)=
\sum_i\lambda_i\ell_i+
\sum_i\{(k_i-\lambda_ia_i)x_i+\lambda_ib_ix_i^2/2\}
+D_\lambda X^2/2.
\tag{A}
\]
Then the exact minimum compensation budget satisfies
\[
B^*=\max_{\lambda\in[0,1]^N}\min_{x\in[0,1]^N}L(x,\lambda).
\tag{B}
\]
Indeed \([z]_+=\max_{0\le\lambda\le1}\lambda z\), so the source objective is \(\max_\lambda L(x,\lambda)\). The box domains are compact and convex; \(L\) is continuous, convex in \(x\), and affine in \(\lambda\). The finite convex epigraph program described in the source has strict feasibility and its Lagrange multipliers on transfer constraints sum to one. Its strong duality therefore gives (B). Equivalently, the convex-concave minimax theorem applies directly to (A).

This formula is constructive. At any fixed \(\lambda\), every coordinate with \(\lambda_i=0\) is zero at an inner minimum: its derivative is \(k_i+D_\lambda X>0\). For the other coordinates, define
\[
x_i(X)=\left[
\frac{\lambda_i a_i-k_i-D_\lambda X}{\lambda_i b_i}
\right]_0^1.
\]
The aggregate \(X_\lambda\) is the unique solution of
\[
X_\lambda=\sum_{\lambda_i>0}x_i(X_\lambda)
\quad\text{on }[0,N].
\tag{C}
\]
To check existence, subtract the right side from \(X\). The resulting continuous function is nonpositive at zero, nonnegative at \(N\), and strictly increasing: its first term strictly increases while every subtracted term is nonincreasing. Hence it has exactly one zero. At that zero, the displayed clipped coordinates satisfy precisely the box first-order conditions for the convex inner problem. They therefore minimize it. If all \(\lambda_i\) vanish, (C) reads \(X=0\), correctly returning no training. If \(D_\lambda=0\), the formula reduces to independent clipped choices.

Any candidate \(\lambda\) now supplies a rigorous lower bound \(L(x(X_\lambda),\lambda)\) on the required budget. Conversely any training vector supplies the primal upper bound
\[
\sum_i k_ix_i+\sum_i[\ell_i-g_i(x)]_+.
\]
Equality certifies global optimality without inspecting every competing policy. This is useful when an approximate policy is proposed: the difference between the two bounds is a genuine optimality gap.

There is also an exact sensitivity interpretation. With other primitives fixed, (B) expresses \(B^*(\ell)\) as a supremum of affine functions of the loss vector \(\ell\). Hence it is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing. If \(\lambda^*\) is a dual optimum at \(\ell\), then for any other nonnegative loss vector \(\ell'\),
\[
B^*(\ell')\ge B^*(\ell)+\lambda^{*T}(\ell'-\ell).
\]
The multiplier is a subgradient of the compensation frontier. Since \(0\le\lambda_i\le1\), one also has
\[
|B^*(\ell')-B^*(\ell)|\le\sum_i|\ell_i'-\ell_i|.
\]
Thus the model's optimal budget cannot move by more than the total absolute revision to measured losses. This bound remains valid at kinks where a worker first becomes exactly compensated.

This is a restricted optimization and sensitivity extension. It retains observable losses, enforceable divisible training, nonnegative transfers and the specified quadratic congestion. It does not add private information, identify spillovers from small experiments, or replace the source's distinction between a Pareto compensation floor and weighted welfare.

title: Exact minimax-regret subsidy under the sharp spatial welfare interval
scope: Policy choice under the source's identified agglomeration interval when national welfare is strictly concave in the subsidy.
significance: Solves minimax regret for the entire sharp identified welfare family, including boundary-constrained oracle policies and an explicit interior regret formula.
body:
# Exact minimax-regret subsidy under the spatial welfare interval

The sharp observational interval in the manuscript identifies an entire family of national welfare curves, not merely a separate interval at one subsidy. This makes it possible to solve a decision problem under the remaining uncertainty. In the strictly concave case, minimax regret has a closed form that handles constrained policy endpoints.

Retain the source's observations and restrictions, and assume
\[
K=(H-g)/H^2+a>0,\qquad S=\bar s.
\]
Let \(\beta=gn_0-\gamma_2\). The sharp interval for \(\gamma_2\) implies the sharp common-parameter family
\[
\beta\in[\beta_L,\beta_U]=[gn_0-U,gn_0-L],\qquad
W_\beta(s)=\beta s/H-Ks^2/2,\quad0\le s\le S.
\tag{A}
\]
The same value of \(\beta\) governs the entire curve. Allowing it to vary independently with each policy would be a different uncertainty model.

If \(\beta\) were known, its unique oracle policy and value would be
\[
s_\beta=\left[\frac{\beta}{HK}\right]_0^S,\qquad
M(\beta)=W_\beta(s_\beta).
\]
For a chosen policy \(s\), define regret \(R_\beta(s)=M(\beta)-W_\beta(s)\). Suppose first that \(\beta_L<\beta_U\). The exact minimax-regret subsidy is
\[
s^{MR}=
\frac{H\{M(\beta_U)-M(\beta_L)\}}{\beta_U-\beta_L}.
\tag{B}
\]
In particular no additional clipping is needed in this formula.

Here is a proof including the boundary cases. The value \(M(\beta)\) is a supremum of affine functions of \(\beta\), hence convex. Therefore, for fixed \(s\), regret is convex in \(\beta\), and its maximum over the interval occurs at one of its endpoints. Write these two regret functions as \(R_L,R_U\). Their difference is
\[
R_U(s)-R_L(s)=M(\beta_U)-M(\beta_L)
-(\beta_U-\beta_L)s/H.
\tag{C}
\]
They cross exactly at the value in (B).

The oracle map \(s_\beta\) is continuous and nondecreasing, and direct differentiation of its three regimes gives \(M'(\beta)=s_\beta/H\), including the joining thresholds. Integrating this derivative shows
\[
s_{\beta_L}\le s^{MR}\le s_{\beta_U}.
\]
Both oracle policies lie in \([0,S]\), proving feasibility of (B). For \(s<s^{MR}\), equation (C) makes \(R_U\) the larger regret. It is decreasing up to its constrained minimizer \(s_{\beta_U}\), which is at least \(s^{MR}\). For \(s>s^{MR}\), the larger regret is \(R_L\), increasing after \(s_{\beta_L}\), which is at most \(s^{MR}\). Their maximum is therefore minimized exactly at the crossing. This reasoning also covers the case where both oracle policies equal zero or both equal \(S\): the crossing is that common endpoint, with zero regret. Strict convexity in \(s\) gives uniqueness.

When both endpoint oracles are interior,
\[
s^{MR}=\frac{\beta_L+\beta_U}{2HK},\qquad
\sup_\beta R_\beta(s^{MR})
=\frac{(\beta_U-\beta_L)^2}{8H^2K}.
\tag{D}
\]
Indeed \(M(\beta)=\beta^2/(2H^2K)\) in that regime; substitution into (B) proves the midpoint rule, and completing the square gives the regret. If the parameter interval collapses to a point, use its known oracle directly rather than the undefined quotient in (B).

This decision criterion differs from maximizing worst-case welfare: (A) implies that maximin welfare uses the lower endpoint \(\beta_L\) and chooses \(s_{\beta_L}\). Minimax regret instead balances losses relative to the policy that each admissible economy would have selected. The report does not choose between those objectives on the policymaker's behalf.

The result relies on the source's sharp common-parameter construction, fixed identities, quasilinearity and constant positive curvature. It does not identify the true agglomeration split, introduce wage-response evidence, or solve unequal-ownership and heterogeneous-welfare extensions. No empirical recommendation or external-literature claim is made.

title: Capacity rents attenuate the task-cost elasticities of aggregate output
scope: Envelope and Euler identities in the source's finite-task CES model with positive task capacity bounds and an unsaturated aggregate resource budget.
significance: Derives exact cost and capacity elasticities, showing their resource-adjusted aggregation weights sum below one by precisely the capacity-shadow-rent share.
body:
# Capacity rents attenuate aggregate task-cost elasticities

The manuscript gives exact unconstrained expenditure weights and a capacity-constrained allocation. Those weights require modification once task capacities bind. Within the same model, a shadow-price identity measures exactly how much total output responsiveness to task costs is attenuated.

Write the productive budget as \(E=R-F>0\). Retain positive costs, weights and capacity bounds, and the source's assumption \(E<\sum_jc_j\bar q_j\), with infinite capacities permitted. Let \(V(c,E,\bar q)\) be optimal CES output, and \(q^*\) its unique allocation from the capacity theorem. Every task is produced positively, and at least one is unsaturated. Let \(m_j=\partial Q(q^*)/\partial q_j\).

The first-order conditions supply a positive resource multiplier \(\lambda\) and nonnegative capacity multipliers \(\nu_j\):
\[
m_j=\lambda c_j+\nu_j,\qquad
\nu_j(\bar q_j-q_j^*)=0.
\tag{A}
\]
For an infinite cap set \(\nu_j=0\). An unsaturated positive coordinate gives \(\lambda=m_j/c_j>0\). The budget binds because output is increasing and not every task can be saturated. The source's clipped allocation satisfies these conditions; concavity makes them sufficient.

Euler's identity for the homogeneous CES aggregator gives
\[
V=\sum_jq_j^*m_j
=\lambda E+\sum_{j:\bar q_j<\infty}\nu_j\bar q_j.
\tag{B}
\]
Thus aggregate output decomposes into a resource shadow value and capacity shadow rents. The latter are optimization values, not additional measured output or an assumed household transfer.

The envelope derivatives, at a regular parameter point, are
\[
\frac{\partial V}{\partial c_j}=-\lambda q_j^*,\quad
\frac{\partial V}{\partial E}=\lambda,\quad
\frac{\partial V}{\partial\bar q_j}=\nu_j
\quad(\bar q_j<\infty).
\tag{C}
\]
They follow by differentiating the Lagrangian \(Q+\lambda(E-\sum c_jq_j)+\sum\nu_j(\bar q_j-q_j)\). No derivative of the chosen quantities enters because the first-order and complementarity conditions cancel those terms. The same statements apply within each fixed active-set region; at switching points one can instead use the associated one-sided envelope sensitivities. The primal optimizer and resource multiplier are uniquely determined here.

Define
\[
s_j=\frac{\lambda c_jq_j^*}{V},\qquad
r_j=\frac{\nu_j\bar q_j}{V}
\]
for finite caps, with \(r_j=0\) at infinite caps. Equations (B) and (C) imply
\[
-\frac{\partial\log V}{\partial\log c_j}=s_j,\qquad
\frac{\partial\log V}{\partial\log E}=\sum_js_j,\qquad
\sum_js_j+\sum_jr_j=1.
\tag{D}
\]
Consequently the cost elasticities sum to at most one, and strictly less than one whenever a capacity has positive shadow value. Without active caps, every \(\nu_j=0\), \(V=E/P(c)\), and \(s_j\) reduces exactly to the manuscript's CES expenditure share. A cap that happens to bind with zero multiplier creates no strict attenuation; that distinction matters at thresholds.

For example, reduce every task cost proportionally while holding physical caps and \(E\) fixed. Equation (D) says that its local output elasticity is \(\lambda E/V\), rather than automatically one. Saved resources can expand unsaturated tasks, but cannot expand the physically fixed task quantities. Conversely, relaxing a valuable cap has elasticity \(r_j\), which the unconstrained task-cost index omits. Since \(E=R-F\), the local loss from an additional unit of deployment cost is \(\partial V/\partial F=-\lambda\).

These formulas give an independent aggregation check for experiments reporting task-level cost reductions. They retain the common-resource model and declared physical caps; they do not identify compute capacity, deployment investment or an empirical TFP accounting map. They neither equate shadow rents with national income nor infer that cap constraints disappear in a transition. The manuscript's bottleneck ceiling and measured-TFP identity remain separate statements.
